claims.claim: Kay says he likes playing variations on other writers, as he plays variations on historical periods in his fiction.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Penguin Canada Q&A on Beyond this Dark House, reproduced at brightweavings.com
claims.quote: I like playing variations on some other writers
claims.page: Questions and Answers on Beyond this Dark House, Q4

claims.feature: other: biography of the Silmarillion year
claims.claim: Locus's biographical note states that Kay and Christopher Tolkien worked on The Silmarillion at Oxford from 1974 to 1975.
claims.source: Locus, biographical note accompanying 'Guy Gavriel Kay: Margins of History', 2025
claims.quote: They worked on the book at Oxford from 1974-75

claims.claim: Allsopp says Dunnett's books are studded with poetry quoted in many languages, a fact her Desert Island Discs persona concealed.
claims.source: Niall Allsopp, 'Dorothy Dunnett's Lymond Chronicles', Slightly Foxed Issue 81, 2024
claims.quote: studded with poetry quoted in Scots, French, Spanish, Italian, Latin
claims.page: article body, Desert Island Discs paragraph

claims.feature: other: competing memories of one event
claims.claim: Kay says that when he switches point of view in Children of Earth and Sky the same conversation is not the same, only resembling its other telling.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: the conversation isn't the same. It bears a resemblance
claims.page: interview, multiple points of view question

claims.feature: other: seam between invention and record
claims.claim: Kay says that if a reader can pick out what is made up and what is real, the storytelling has been botched.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: if a reader can pick out what's made up and what's real
claims.page: interview, Bring Up the Bodies question

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: Rateliff says he knows of no evidence that Kay wrote any of the published Silmarillion.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Kay and Christopher', Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 6 February 2020
claims.quote: I don't know of any evidence that Kay wrote any of it

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: Rateliff judges it far more likely that Kay helped in the sorting and sequencing of the manuscripts.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Kay and Christopher', Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 6 February 2020
claims.quote: Kay helped in the sorting and sequencing of the manuscripts

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: Rateliff says Kay also served as a sounding board whose advice Christopher Tolkien sometimes took.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Kay and Christopher', Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 6 February 2020
claims.quote: I think Kay also served as a sounding board

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: Rateliff ranks Kay's input to the published Silmarillion above that of Clyde Kilby and Taum Santoski.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Kay and Christopher', Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 6 February 2020
claims.quote: I think Kilby had the least input and Kay probably the most

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: Noad thinks it reasonable to suppose that Kay's nascent creativity in narrative played a part in the published Silmarillion.
claims.source: Charles Noad, comments published by John D. Rateliff, Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 27 January 2020
claims.quote: Kay's nascent creativity in the matter of narrative played a part

claims.feature: other: silence about the editing method
claims.claim: Noad says the details of Kay's contribution will probably never be known unless Kay breaks his silence on the matter.
claims.source: Charles Noad, comments published by John D. Rateliff, Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 27 January 2020
claims.quote: Kay one day breaks his silence on the matter

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: Noad says the passage narrating Thingol's death in the published Silmarillion is unquestionably an invention of the editors.
claims.source: Charles Noad, comments published by John D. Rateliff, Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 27 January 2020
claims.quote: the passage about Thingol's death is an invention of the editors

claims.feature: other: narrative craft versus textual editing
claims.claim: Noad argues that producing a finished narrative from edited texts requires a degree of creativity distinct from textual editing, and identifies that as where Kay enters.
claims.source: Charles Noad, quoted from an archived Tolkien Plaza review by an anonymous commenter on Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 29 January 2020
claims.quote: Here I think is where Guy Gavriel Kay enters the picture

claims.feature: other: narrative craft versus textual editing
claims.claim: Noad states that it was Kay's idea to produce a finished narrative rather than a scholarly version of the Silmarillion material.
claims.source: Charles Noad, quoted from an archived Tolkien Plaza review by an anonymous commenter on Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 29 January 2020
claims.quote: Kay's idea to produce a finished narrative

claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion
claims.claim: A commenter reports that Shippey, Flieger and Rosebury each mistook the editors' scene of Thingol's death for J.R.R. Tolkien's own work.
claims.source: Anonymous commenter on John D. Rateliff's Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 26 January 2020
claims.quote: mistakenly referred to the scene of Thingol's death as J.R.R. Tolkien's work
